passagesDetail.text: [calm] We believe India buys its weapons. Some of it does. But look at what is being made. [long pause] [long pause] In Episode 4, we saw how a defence system senses, decides and steers. This time, we ask a plainer question: who makes the thing? [long pause] [long pause] Not who designs it. Who makes the thousands of parts, in thousands of workshops, and makes them well enough to trust?

[calm] That is the story of how a country goes from buying to building. [long pause] [long pause] There is a reason to care that is not about engineering. [long pause] [long pause] In twenty fourteen to fifteen, India's defence production was about forty-six thousand crore rupees.

[calm] In twenty twenty-five to twenty-six, it was one point seven eight lakh crore. [long pause] [long pause] A lakh crore is a trillion rupees. So that is one point seven eight trillion rupees, a record, the government said in June. [long pause] [long pause] To see where that money goes, we need three ideas. Idea one: many small makers make one machine.

[calm] Think of a car. It is not built in one workshop. Hundreds of small shops make the seats, the glass and the screws, and one factory puts them together. [long pause] [long pause] A defence machine is the same. About sixteen thousand small and medium businesses are part of India's defence industry. [long pause] [long pause] Picture a web, with a big factory at the centre and small makers around it, each doing one thing well.

[calm] Idea two: nothing ships until it passes. We tell you this because a thousand parts are only as good as the worst one. [long pause] [long pause] Think of school exams. You do not move up because you tried. You move up because you passed. [long pause] [long pause] Every part is tested against a standard, and the whole machine is tested again. This is the proof idea from Episode 2, only now it runs in every workshop.

[calm] Idea three: making one is not the same as making a thousand. Why does that matter? Because a defence force needs thousands, on time. [long pause] [long pause] Think of baking. One cake at home is a hobby. A thousand cakes a day is a bakery, with ovens, shifts and a steady supply of flour. [long pause] [long pause] To scale, a country needs factories, trained workers and a steady flow of orders. In twenty twenty-four to twenty-five, the government signed a record one hundred and ninety-three defence contracts, worth more than two lakh crore rupees, and about ninety-two percent went to domestic industry.

[calm] Now, the part that is not engineering. [long pause] [long pause] In twenty twenty-five to twenty-six, India's defence exports reached a record thirty-eight thousand four hundred and twenty-four crore rupees. [long pause] [long pause] In twenty fourteen, the same exports were under two thousand crore. That is more than nineteen times as much.

[calm] Here the small-base effect matters. When you start from almost nothing, any growth looks enormous. [long pause] [long pause] So hold two numbers together. Exports are about a fifth of what India produces. That is real growth from a small start, and still a long way from the whole. [long pause] [long pause] What India can do: produce at a record level, with thousands of small makers, and, the Defence Minister says, reach more than eighty countries.

[calm] What it cannot yet do: reach its own targets. The aim for twenty twenty-nine is three lakh crore in production and fifty thousand crore in exports. [long pause] [long pause] A target is not a result. Between today and that aim, there are about three years. [long pause] [long pause] Think back to the cake in Episode 2.

[calm] A country can buy the cake, bake from someone else's recipe, write a recipe together, or write its own. [long pause] [long pause] Countries often mix all four, for different parts, at different times. [long pause] [long pause] Building more at home does not mean buying nothing. It means choosing what to buy, and why.

[calm] A fictional Sunday: a small part fails on a ship far from port. [long pause] [long pause] If a workshop nearby makes that part, a replacement can arrive by morning. If not, it waits for a delivery. [long pause] [long pause] A factory floor is part of the defence. It just does not look like one.

[calm] One idea about people: we trust big multiples. [long pause] [long pause] Nineteen times sounds like a victory. The honest question is always: nineteen times what? [long pause] [long pause] Ask it of every record you hear, including the ones in this series.

[calm] Five episodes, one chain. [long pause] [long pause] An air defence system, a fighter engine, a floating airport, a defence that senses and decides, and the workshops under all of them. [long pause] [long pause] In each one, India has built a great deal, and has something left to build.
[calm] India has learned to build. The question for the next decade: what will it choose never to buy again?
